problem: Social navigation work mostly models pedestrian position and trajectory; robots' intent cues such as LED turn signals are hard for people to interpret without prior exposure (passive demonstrations), and robots do not read human gaze.
motivation: Gaze is a natural, implicit cue humans use to signal and read walking intent, so it may be interpreted without training. Prior LED turn signals only worked when participants had previously seen the signal being used (demonstration + LED: 20% conflict vs 90-100% otherwise).
key_idea: Use gaze as a bidirectional social cue in navigation: a robot displays a virtual head turn to signal its intended lane, and reads human gaze yaw plus position to predict pedestrians' goals.
insight: Human field study shows congruent gaze cuts conflicts (25% vs 48% incongruent, 28% no gaze), so gaze carries real navigational information. On the robot, a virtual head-turn cue got 50% conflict-free passes vs 0% for LEDs without demonstration, meaning gaze is more readily interpretable than an arbitrary signal. The VR study suggests gaze yaw plus position predicts the goal earlier than other cues, but the sample is small (7 participants).
method: LED turn signal baseline: 0.475 m strips with 14 LEDs on the BWIBot chassis blink to indicate the lane the robot will shift into (re-implementation of Fernandez et al.)
Virtual head gaze cue: 3D-rendered Maki head (Unity, ROSBridgeLib) on a 21.5-inch monitor; the head turns 16.5° over 1.5 s toward the intended lane and holds; eyes are not animated

Three-lane hallway model with distance thresholds: d_signal=4 m (leg detector + LiDAR range), d_execute=2.75 m, d_conflict=1 m; robot speed 0.75 m/s; always moves to the left lane so success reflects cue interpretation
Human field study: confederates use congruent, incongruent or no gaze (phone) in a busy hallway; an observer annotates conflicts (partial, quick shift, full), 220 interactions

Gaze-based goal prediction: VR headset with eye tracker; multivariate Gaussian time-series model over gaze yaw and position predicts which of 5 goals a walker heads to, cross-validated per participant (7 participants)

setting.backbone: none for the robot cue (hand-designed signalling and lane logic); multivariate Gaussian time-series model for VR goal prediction
setting.training_data: VR gaze predictor trained on data from 7 participants (leave-one-participant-out); robot cue is not learned
setting.observation: Robot: on-board LiDAR + leg detector for person detection; VR study: headset eye-tracker gaze yaw and position
setting.action_space: three-lane hallway lane changes (left/middle/right) at 0.75 m/s with head-turn or LED signal
setting.simulator: Unity VR environment for gaze prediction study; real hallway built from cubicle furniture for robot study

numbers_note: Not an embodied-navigation benchmark paper; results are human-study conflict rates (see results), no standard benchmark metrics.
results: In the robot hallway study, gaze gave 8/16 (50%) conflict-free passes vs 0/11 (0%) for LEDs without passive demonstration (Bonferroni md=-0.50, p=0.004). The human field study found conflicts of 25% congruent, 48% incongruent and 28% no gaze, with congruent significantly better than the others. In the VR study gaze yaw plus position predicted the goal earlier than the other cues tested.
limitations: Small samples (27 robot participants after exclusions, 7 VR participants) and a single controlled hallway; the gaze predictor only handles a discrete set of goals
The robot only signals; it does not yet react to human gaze, and the study forces left-lane passing to isolate cue interpretation
Draft workshop paper with unfinished sections (VR subsection placeholder) and inconsistent conflict statistics (e.g. 15% vs 25% for congruent)
builds_on: Fernandez et al. 2018 passive demonstration LED turn signals
Holman et al. 2021 VR gaze prediction
